notes: Scope: people of code and cryptography who shaped the privacy debate, 1976–2026 — public-key cryptography (Diffie, Hellman), anonymity and pseudonymity (Chaum, Syverson, Dingledine, Mathewson), user-held encryption (Zimmermann, Marlinspike), the cypherpunks (Hughes, May, Gilmore), the crypto wars (Blaze on Clipper, Bernstein on export controls), cryptocurrency's privacy model (Nakamoto, Back) and data-release privacy (Sweeney, Dwork). Method: each person and event was researched one at a time; every quote was copied from the fetched page and checked with tools/fetch-text.py --check (FOUND). Where the helper was blocked but curl could read the page (blog.whatsapp.com), the helper's cache was primed with the curl copy so --check ran on the real text; this is noted on that source. Primary texts preferred: the original papers (IEEE Trans. IT 1976, CACM 1981/1985, NRL 1996, USENIX 2004, bitcoin.pdf), mailing-list archives (cypherpunks 1992, or-dev 2002, metzdowd 2008), court records (9th Cir. Bernstein; C.D. Cal. status report in Apple/FBI; COPA v Wright), official statements (Clinton White House 1993; GCHQ; Census Bureau) and the actors' own sites. Could not verify / gaps: the ACM Turing Award pages (403) — Stanford's copy used instead; The New York Times's 2 June 1994 Clipper-flaw story (403; dated via an MIT course index); the Forbes 2010 Whisper Systems launch story (403; kept PENDING, used only for a location note); justice.gov's copy of the Apple status report (401; a law professor's hosted copy used); the 16 February 2016 order itself (scanned image, no text layer); DAO 216-26's number (only from search summaries). Location caveats: Satoshi Nakamoto and Adam Back have no verifiable place (lat/lng null), and the Bitcoin white-paper event is online-only (lat/lng null — do not map). Moxie Marlinspike, the Signal 2015 event and Let's Encrypt are placed at the IRS-listed cities of their organisations (Mountain View; Sacramento), which may be registered rather than operating addresses. Balance: controversies noted where on the record — May's manifesto on illicit markets; Gilmore's 2021 removal from EFF's board (both sides' words); DigiCash's commercial failure; the withdrawn Bernstein panel opinion; the 2026 Commerce order banning 'noise infusion' at the Census Bureau. Images: 17 openly licensed Wikimedia Commons files (public domain, CC0, CC BY, CC BY-SA), licences read from the Commons API extmetadata, downloaded as standard-size thumbnails (Wikimedia rejects script requests for originals) and converted to JPEG q82; alt text written after viewing each file. Portraits exist for 15 of 17 people — none was found for Timothy C. May, and none is sought for the pseudonymous Satoshi Nakamoto; Martin Hellman's is a 2008 RSA Conference panel photo in which he is third from left; Eric Hughes's shows a masked figure with a 'Luther Blissett' badge whose identity rests on the uploader's description. Two non-portrait images illustrate events: the 2004 Tor circuit diagram and Adam Back's 1997 'munitions' T-shirt. Known gaps: Julian Assange, Bruce Schneier, Zooko Wilcox-O'Hearn, Ron Rivest and Tim Berners-Lee (Solid) were considered and left out to keep the set to well-sourced cards; GCHQ pages are undated.

people.name: Whitfield Diffie

keyWork.title: New Directions in Cryptography (with Martin E. Hellman), IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, vol. IT-22, no. 6

people.contribution: With Martin Hellman, Diffie published the 1976 paper that introduced public-key cryptography and digital signatures to the open literature. The scheme lets two people who have never met agree on a secret over an insecure channel, removing the need for a courier or other secure channel to deliver keys in advance. Diffie was a part-time researcher at Stanford at the time.
people.quote: Cryptography is the one indispensable security technique … if the government had succeeded in blocking people from having strong cryptographic systems … it would have meant you could not have had security on the Internet.

people.influence: Public-key cryptography moved strong encryption out of classified government research and into the open, provoking the first clash between academic cryptographers and the NSA — later called the first 'crypto war' — and became the basis of Internet security.
people.thread: In a public-key system each person generates and keeps a secret key and publishes only the matching public key, so the ability to read one's messages rests with the individual rather than with a central key authority.

people.name: David Chaum
people.roles: cryptographer · inventor of mix networks and blind-signature e-cash · founder of DigiCash and the IACR

keyWork.title: Security without Identification: Transaction Systems to Make Big Brother Obsolete, Communications of the ACM 28(10), pp. 1030–1044

people.contribution: As a Berkeley researcher, Chaum published in February 1981 a public-key technique — the 'mix' — that hides who is writing to whom as well as what is said, without a universally trusted authority, and that supports untraceable return addresses and digital pseudonyms. His 1985 Communications of the ACM article proposed that individuals use a different, unlinkable 'digital pseudonym' with each organisation, held on a personal 'card computer'. He founded DigiCash to commercialise anonymous electronic cash; after bank pilots that never passed the pilot stage, the company filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in November 1998.
people.quote: Computerization is robbing individuals of the ability to monitor and control the ways information about them is used.

people.name: Philip R. Zimmermann

keyWork.title: Pretty Good Privacy (PGP) 1.0 and its user's guide essay 'Why I Wrote PGP'

people.contribution: Zimmermann wrote Pretty Good Privacy, public-key email encryption for ordinary personal computers, and on 5 June 1991 sent the first release to friends who posted it to Peacenet, a Usenet source-code newsgroup and bulletin boards. He said a 1991 Senate anticrime bill urging that communications systems let the government obtain plaintext is what led him to publish it free. PGP 2.0 (September 1992) added what he calls 'the now-famous PGP trust model'; soon after, US Customs opened an export investigation that ran three years and was closed without charges in January 1996.
people.quote: If privacy is outlawed, only outlaws will have privacy.

people.influence: PGP put strong public-key encryption into the hands of individuals worldwide, and the government's investigation of its spread helped ignite, in Zimmermann's words, 'a controversy that would eventually lead to the demise of the US export restrictions on strong cryptography'.

people.name: Eric Hughes
people.roles: mathematician · cypherpunk co-founder · author of 'A Cypherpunk's Manifesto'
people.contribution: Hughes and Timothy C. May instigated the first physical cypherpunk meeting in autumn 1992; Hughes then maintained the cypherpunks mailing list, which ran on John Gilmore's toad.com machine, and moderated the monthly meetings, the second of which was held at Gilmore's Cygnus offices. Within days of the list's start he posted the Perl script for a 'hopping' remailer he had written to forward mail stripped of its sender. His 'A Cypherpunk's Manifesto', dated 9 March 1993, defined privacy as selective self-disclosure and argued it would need anonymous transaction systems built and distributed by the people who wanted it.
people.quote: Privacy is necessary for an open society in the electronic age. Privacy is not secrecy. … Privacy is the power to selectively reveal oneself to the world.

people.influence: The manifesto's credo that 'Cypherpunks write code' — privacy secured by building and distributing tools rather than by waiting for institutions to grant it — framed a movement whose members, as Wired reported in 1993, were 'hard at work creating remailers' and discussing anonymous digital money.
people.thread: Hughes's manifesto locates privacy with the individual rather than institutions: 'We cannot expect governments, corporations, or other large, faceless organizations to grant us privacy out of their beneficence' — and asks that each party to a transaction learn 'only … that which is directly necessary', an early statement of data minimisation by design.

people.name: Matt Blaze
people.place: AT&T Bell Laboratories, Murray Hill, New Jersey

keyWork.title: Protocol Failure in the Escrowed Encryption Standard (2nd ACM Conference on Computer and Communications Security, Fairfax, Virginia, November 1994)

people.contribution: Blaze worked at AT&T Bell Laboratories; AT&T was the first, and ultimately the only, company to produce a full product (the TSD-3600 telephone security device) based on the government's Clipper escrow system. Blaze examined the Escrowed Encryption Standard and a prototype PCMCIA escrow card. He found that the Law Enforcement Access Field meant to give government wiretappers the session key was protected by only a 16-bit checksum, so a 'rogue' device could forge a valid-looking field by brute force in about 2^16 tries and communicate with legitimate Clipper devices while bypassing escrow. The paper was written in April 1994 and reported on the front page of The New York Times in June 1994.
people.quote: While my paper may have helped accelerate its demise, key escrow would not have been likely to succeed even if the Clipper escrow mechanism had been more robust than it was.

people.name: Paul F. Syverson

keyWork.title: Hiding Routing Information (with David M. Goldschlag and Michael G. Reed), Workshop on Information Hiding, Cambridge, UK

people.contribution: With David Goldschlag and Michael Reed at the Naval Research Laboratory's Center for High Assurance Computer Systems, Syverson began work on onion routing in late 1995 and presented the first design at the Information Hiding Workshop in Cambridge in May 1996: traffic is wrapped in layers of encryption and relayed through proxies so that no one but the initiator's proxy knows more than the previous and next hop. In the early 2000s he worked with Roger Dingledine and Nick Mathewson on the second-generation design, Tor, published with them at USENIX Security in 2004. He has stressed that the aim was to separate identification from routing rather than to guarantee anonymity.
people.quote: Applications can (and usually should) identify themselves to each other. But, the use of a public network should not automatically reveal the identities of communicating parties. The goal here is anonymous routing, not anonymity.

keyWork.title: Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System

people.contribution: On 31 October 2008 a person or group writing as Satoshi Nakamoto announced 'a new electronic cash system that's fully peer-to-peer, with no trusted third party' on the Cryptography mailing list and published the Bitcoin white paper, which uses a proof-of-work system 'similar to Adam Back's Hashcash' and cites Wei Dai's b-money. Because every transaction is announced publicly, the paper abandoned the banking model of privacy through restricted access and proposed instead to keep public keys unlinked to identities, recommending a new key pair for each transaction while conceding that some linking was unavoidable. The author's identity has never been established; in 2024 England's High Court declared that Craig Wright, who had claimed the role, is not Satoshi Nakamoto.
people.quote: The necessity to announce all transactions publicly precludes this method, but privacy can still be maintained by breaking the flow of information in another place: by keeping public keys anonymous.

quoteSource.title: Satoshi Nakamoto, 'Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System', section 10 'Privacy'
quoteSource.quote: The necessity to announce all transactions publicly precludes this method, but privacy can still be maintained by breaking the flow of information in another place: by keeping public keys anonymous.
quoteSource.note: 'This method' refers to the preceding sentence: 'The traditional banking model achieves a level of privacy by limiting access to information to the parties involved and the trusted third party.' keyWork.title: Differential Privacy (33rd International Colloquium on Automata, Languages and Programming, ICALP 2006)

people.contribution: Working at Microsoft Research, Dwork showed in 2006 that the long-standing goal for statistical databases — that nothing about an individual be learnable that could not be learned without the database — cannot be achieved, and proposed instead 'differential privacy': any given disclosure should be almost equally likely whether or not a person's data are included. With colleagues she developed methods that add calibrated random noise to statistics to meet that guarantee. The technique is used by Apple on its devices and was the basis of the Disclosure Avoidance System for the 2020 US Census; she received the US National Medal of Science in January 2025.
people.quote: The risk to one's privacy, or in general, any type of risk, such as the risk of being denied automobile insurance, should not substantially increase as a result of participating in a statistical database.

events.summary: Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman of Stanford University published 'New Directions in Cryptography' in the November 1976 issue of IEEE Transactions on Information Theory (manuscript received 3 June 1976). It proposed public-key cryptosystems, in which each user publishes an enciphering key and keeps a separate deciphering key secret, and a method for two parties to agree a key over a public channel. The NSA later campaigned to limit the spread of the authors' research, and one NSA employee warned publishers the authors could face prison under arms-export law.
events.significance: It made confidential communication possible between strangers without a trusted courier, putting the secret key in the hands of each individual user.

events.title: Phil Zimmermann releases Pretty Good Privacy (PGP) 1.0
events.summary: On 5 June 1991 Phil Zimmermann sent the first release of PGP, email encryption software for MS-DOS, to friends for uploading: Allan Hoeltje posted it to Peacenet, and Kelly Goen to a Usenet source-code newsgroup (marked 'US only') and bulletin-board systems; Zimmermann could not recall whether the Internet postings began on 5 or 6 June. Zimmermann said Senate Bill 266, a 1991 anticrime bill whose non-binding resolution would have had communications systems let the government obtain plaintext, led him to publish it free.
events.significance: Strong public-key encryption became something an individual could download and run, rather than a service granted by a government or a bank.

sources.title: PGP Marks 10th Anniversary
sources.quote: It was on this day in 1991 that I sent the first release of PGP to a couple of my friends for uploading to the Internet.
sources.note: Next sentence: 'First, I sent it to Allan Hoeltje, who posted it to Peacenet, an ISP that specialized in grassroots political organizations, mainly in the peace movement.' The page also says Kelly Goen uploaded it to a Usenet newsgroup marked 'US only', and 'I don't recall if the postings to the Internet began on June 5th or 6th.'

sources.title: Why I Wrote PGP — part of the original 1991 PGP User's Guide (updated in 1999)
sources.quote: It was this bill that led me to publish PGP electronically for free that year, shortly before the measure was defeated after vigorous protest by civil libertarians and industry groups.

events.locationNote: Coordinates: Boulder, Colorado, where Zimmermann signed the 1991 user's-guide essay. The uploads were made by friends elsewhere; the page does not name their locations.

events.title: US prosecutors close the PGP export investigation without charges
events.place: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of California, San Jose
events.summary: On 11 January 1996 Assistant U.S. Attorney William Keane in San Jose told Zimmermann's lawyer, Philip Dubois, that Zimmermann would not be prosecuted over the June 1991 Usenet posting of PGP, ending a three-year investigation. U.S. Attorney Michael J. Yamaguchi announced that his office had declined prosecution of any individuals and gave no reasons. Dubois speculated the government may not have wanted to risk a ruling that posting software on a US Internet site is not an 'export', or that the export-control law was unconstitutional.
events.significance: The case made the export-control treatment of encryption as a munition a public controversy about whether citizens may communicate privately.

sources.institution: Philip Zimmermann (philzimmermann.com), reproducing the signed news release of defence counsel Philip L. Dubois
sources.title: Significant Moments in PGP's History: Zimmermann Case Dropped
sources.quote: Yesterday morning, I received word from Assistant U.S. Attorney William Keane in San Jose, California, that the government's three-year investigation of Philip Zimmermann is over.
sources.note: Dubois's release is dated 'Fri, 12 Jan 1996'; Zimmermann's own Cypherpunks-list post is signed '11 Jan 96'.

sources.institution: IEEE Computer Society Technical Committee on Security and Privacy, Cipher newsletter
sources.title: Case Closed on Zimmermann PGP Investigation
sources.quote: Zimmermann maintained thoughout the investigation that he did not put the software on the Internet.
sources.note: The brief says Keane 'announced on January 11' that he had decided to drop the investigation, citing reports in the New York Times and Wall Street Journal.

events.locationNote: Coordinates: federal building, San Jose, where Assistant U.S. Attorney Keane was based (approximate).

events.title: The cypherpunks mailing list opens
events.place: San Francisco Bay Area (list maintained from Berkeley; hosted on John Gilmore's toad.com machine)
events.summary: After a first physical meeting instigated by Timothy C. May and Eric Hughes in early autumn 1992, Hughes welcomed members to 'a real mailing list', cypherpunks@toad.com, on the evening of 21 September 1992 (Pacific time), thanking John Gilmore for machine space. The same message announced a second meeting for 10 October 1992 at Cygnus's new offices. Within four days Hughes had posted code for a 'hopping' anonymous remailer.
events.significance: The list became the meeting place of programmers who treated privacy as something to be built into software and handed to individuals, rather than granted by institutions.

sources.title: Eric Hughes to cypherpunks@toad.com, 'No Subject' (list welcome message)
sources.quote: Welcome to the cypherpunks mailing list. We have a real mailing list now, and not just a mail alias on my account. Thanks to John Gilmore for space on hoptoad and Hugh Daniel for setting things up.
sources.note: Raw date 'Mon, 21 Sep 92 22:47:51 PDT' (22 September UTC). The message also says: 'Second Meeting -- October 10, 1992 The second meeting will be held at the new Cygnus offices.' The archive's September 1992 index lists one earlier post (21 Sep 1992, from Russell E. Whitaker), consistent with Hughes's remark that a mail alias existed before the 'real mailing list'.

sources.title: Steven Levy, 'Crypto Rebels'
sources.quote: The first physical Cypherpunk meeting occurred early last autumn at the instigation of two software engineers who had developed an interest in crypto.
sources.note: The article names the two as Tim May and Eric Hughes. wired.com dates the web copy 1993-02-01; print issue 1.02 (May/June 1993).

events.locationNote: Coordinates: Berkeley, California, where Hughes maintained the list from his soda.berkeley.edu account. The list server (toad.com) belonged to John Gilmore; meetings were held at Cygnus Support's offices near US 101 in Silicon Valley.

events.title: Eric Hughes writes 'A Cypherpunk's Manifesto'
events.summary: Eric Hughes signed 'A Cypherpunk's Manifesto' on 9 March 1993 from his soda.berkeley.edu address. It distinguished privacy from secrecy, defined it as 'the power to selectively reveal oneself to the world', argued that an open society needs anonymous transaction systems, and declared that 'Cypherpunks write code'.
events.significance: It recast privacy as selective disclosure controlled by the individual and enforced by software — a conceptual ancestor of person-held, machine-enforced terms.

sources.title: Eric Hughes, 'A Cypherpunk's Manifesto'
sources.quote: Privacy is necessary for an open society in the electronic age. Privacy is not secrecy. … Privacy is the power to selectively reveal oneself to the world.
sources.note: Signature line: 'Eric Hughes <hughes@soda.berkeley.edu> 9 March 1993'. Also on the page: 'Cypherpunks write code.'

events.locationNote: Coordinates: Berkeley, California (Hughes's berkeley.edu address); the manifesto was circulated online.

events.title: The White House announces the Clipper chip and key escrow
events.place: The White House, Office of the Press Secretary, Washington, D.C.
events.summary: On 16 April 1993 the Clinton White House announced a 'voluntary program' built around the 'Clipper Chip', a government-designed microcircuit to encrypt telephone calls. Each device's two unique keys would be deposited in two separate 'key-escrow' databases established by the Attorney General, accessible to officials with legal authority to wiretap, and the Attorney General would buy several thousand devices. The chip used the NSA-designed Skipjack cipher with an 80-bit key and sent an encrypted copy of each session key at the start of every call.
events.significance: Key escrow proposed that the individual's key be held in advance by the state — the opposite of user-held keys — and the backlash defined the 1990s 'crypto wars'.

sources.institution: The White House, Office of the Press Secretary (Clinton White House archive, National Archives)
sources.title: Statement by the Press Secretary (Clipper Chip encryption initiative)
sources.quote: When the device is manufactured, the two keys will be deposited separately in two "key-escrow" data bases that will be established by the Attorney General. Access to these keys will be limited to government officials with legal authorization to conduct a wiretap.
sources.note: Opening sentence: 'The President today announced a new initiative that will bring the Federal Government together with industry in a voluntary program to improve the security and privacy of telephone communications while meeting the legitimate needs of law enforcement.'

sources.institution: Matt Blaze (mattblaze.org), author copy of ACSAC 2011 paper
sources.title: Key Escrow from a Safe Distance: Looking Back at the Clipper Chip
sources.quote: called Skipjack, designed by the National Security Agency and using an 80 bit key.
sources.note: Full sentence: 'Clipper was intended as a drop-in replacement for a standard DES chip, but with a new symmetric-key cipher algorithm, called Skipjack, designed by the National Security Agency and using an 80 bit key.' (a PDF line break inside 'drop-in' defeats --check on the whole sentence).

events.locationNote: Coordinates: the White House, where the Press Secretary's statement was issued.

events.title: Matt Blaze shows Clipper's key escrow can be bypassed
events.place: AT&T Bell Laboratories, Murray Hill, New Jersey
events.summary: In April 1994 Matt Blaze of AT&T Bell Laboratories wrote 'Protocol Failure in the Escrowed Encryption Standard', showing that the Law Enforcement Access Field (LEAF) carrying the escrowed session key was protected by only a 16-bit checksum. A rogue device could therefore search about 2^16 possibilities for a LEAF that passed the check and talk to legitimate Clipper devices without giving the government a usable key. The New York Times reported the flaw on 2 June 1994; the paper was presented at the ACM Conference on Computer and Communications Security in Fairfax, Virginia, in November 1994.
events.significance: It showed in public that a mandated back door could be engineered around, strengthening the case for letting individuals hold their own keys.

sources.institution: Matt Blaze (mattblaze.org), pre-print of paper for the 2nd ACM Conference on Computer and Communications Security
sources.title: Protocol Failure in the Escrowed Encryption Standard
sources.quote: This paper outlines various techniques that enable cryptographic communication among EES processors without transmission of the valid LEAF.
sources.note: Also: 'The LEAF checksum is, in fact, 16 bits.' Footnote: 'This is a pre-print of a paper to appear at the 2nd ACM Conference on Computer and Communications Security, Fairfax, VA, November 1994.'

sources.institution: Matt Blaze (mattblaze.org), author copy of ACSAC 2011 paper
sources.title: Key Escrow from a Safe Distance: Looking Back at the Clipper Chip
sources.quote: The only thing stopping you was a 16 bit exhaustive search, a very low barrier even in 1993.
sources.note: Blaze: 'In April, 1994, I wrote a paper about all this'; the Times story ran at 'the top of the front page'.

sources.institution: MIT course 6.805 (Ethics and the Law on the Electronic Frontier) reading index
sources.title: Selected items on Clipper — 1994
sources.quote: June 2, 1994, New York Times, "Scientist Finds Flaw In Code Technology"
sources.note: The New York Times article itself (John Markoff) was not read: nytimes.com returned 403.

events.locationNote: Coordinates: AT&T Bell Laboratories, Murray Hill, New Jersey, Blaze's affiliation on the paper.

events.title: Naval Research Laboratory scientists publish onion routing
events.place: U.S. Naval Research Laboratory, Center for High Assurance Computer Systems, Washington, D.C.
events.summary: David Goldschlag, Michael Reed and Paul Syverson of the U.S. Naval Research Laboratory, who had begun the work in late 1995, presented 'Hiding Routing Information' at the Workshop on Information Hiding in Cambridge, UK, in May 1996. Their 'onion routing' architecture relayed traffic through proxy servers so that no one but the initiator's proxy knew more than the previous and next hop, and a prototype already worked with web (HTTP) proxies. The design built on David Chaum's layered mix of 1981.
events.significance: It carried Chaum's idea of hiding who talks to whom from e-mail to the interactive web, the lineage that leads to Tor.

sources.title: D. M. Goldschlag, M. G. Reed and P. F. Syverson, 'Hiding Routing Information', Workshop on Information Hiding, Cambridge, UK, May 1996
sources.quote: This implies that neither the respondent nor his proxy server nor any external observer need know the identity of the initiator or his proxy server.
sources.note: Abstract also: 'This prototype works with HTTP (World Wide Web) proxies.' The related-work section says Chaum [1] defines a layered object 'that routes data through intermediate nodes' (the PDF text layer splits 'object' and garbles the 'fi' ligature in 'defines').

sources.institution: U.S. Naval Research Laboratory / ACSAC 2011 (keynote paper, public domain)
sources.title: Paul Syverson, 'A Peel of Onion'
sources.quote: We (David Goldschlag, Michael Reed, and I) began work on onion routing in late 1995

events.locationNote: Coordinates: the Naval Research Laboratory, Washington, D.C., where the authors worked. The paper was presented at the Information Hiding workshop in Cambridge, UK.

events.title: The Tor onion-routing network goes live as free software
events.place: Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, Massachusetts
events.summary: On 20 September 2002 Roger Dingledine, writing from an MIT address, told the or-dev list that 'the onion routing network is functional and deployed' and invited testers to download tor-0.0.0; the Tor Project dates the initial deployment to October 2002, when its code was released under a free-software licence. By the end of 2003 the network had about a dozen volunteer relays; Dingledine, Nick Mathewson and Paul Syverson published the design at USENIX Security in August 2004, the Electronic Frontier Foundation began funding the work in 2004, and the Tor Project became a 501(c)(3) nonprofit in 2006.
events.significance: Anonymity moved from a laboratory prototype to a public, volunteer-run network that anyone could use without asking permission.

sources.title: Roger Dingledine, 'pre-alpha: run an onion proxy now!'
sources.quote: The onion routing network is functional and deployed. It's not terribly diverse yet, but heck, it's just for show for now.
sources.note: Header: 'From : Roger Dingledine < arma@mit.edu >', 'Date : Fri, 20 Sep 2002 17:14:01 -0400'.

sources.title: History
sources.quote: That's why in October 2002 when the Tor network was initially deployed, its code was released under a free and open software license. By the end of 2003, the network had about a dozen volunteer nodes, mostly in the U.S., plus one in Germany.
sources.note: Same page: 'Recognizing the benefit of Tor to digital rights, the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) began funding Roger's and Nick's work on Tor in 2004. In 2006, the Tor Project, Inc., a 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization, was founded to maintain Tor's development.' The one-month difference from the mailing-list date is unexplained.

sources.institution: USENIX Association, Proceedings of the 13th USENIX Security Symposium (San Diego, 9–13 August 2004)
sources.title: R. Dingledine, N. Mathewson and P. Syverson, 'Tor: The Second-Generation Onion Router'
sources.quote: We present Tor, a circuit-based low-latency anonymous communication service.

events.locationNote: Coordinates: MIT, Cambridge, Massachusetts (Dingledine's arma@mit.edu address on the announcement). The network itself ran on volunteer relays.

events.title: 'Satoshi Nakamoto' publishes the Bitcoin white paper
events.summary: On 31 October 2008 a pseudonymous author, Satoshi Nakamoto, announced on the Cryptography mailing list 'a new electronic cash system that's fully peer-to-peer, with no trusted third party' and linked the white paper 'Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System'. Its privacy section conceded that announcing every transaction publicly ruled out the banks' model of restricted access, and proposed instead keeping public keys unlinked to identities, using a new key pair for each transaction; it acknowledged that multi-input transactions would still link addresses to a common owner.
events.significance: It replaced the trusted intermediary with keys held by individuals, while showing that a public ledger offers pseudonymity, not anonymity.

sources.title: Satoshi Nakamoto, 'Bitcoin P2P e-cash paper'
sources.quote: I've been working on a new electronic cash system that's fully peer-to-peer, with no trusted third party.
sources.note: Archive header: 'Fri Oct 31 14:10:00 EDT 2008'.

sources.title: Satoshi Nakamoto, 'Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System', section 10 'Privacy'
sources.quote: As an additional firewall, a new key pair should be used for each transaction to keep them from being linked to a common owner. Some linking is still unavoidable with multi-input transactions, which necessarily reveal that their inputs were owned by the same owner.

events.locationNote: Online-only and pseudonymous: no verifiable place. The mailing list ran on a machine of Perry Metzger's company, Metzger, Dowdeswell & Co. LLC (https://www.metzdowd.com/pipermail/cryptography/2003-April/004484.html), whose location was not verified. Coordinates deliberately left empty — do not map, or map only as 'online'.

events.title: TextSecure and RedPhone become Signal
events.place: Open Whisper Systems (online; Signal's organisation is registered in Mountain View, California)
events.summary: Whisper Systems, a mobile-security company, was acquired by Twitter in late 2011; Twitter released some of its software under the GPLv3 open-source licence, and from January 2013 continued development was hosted as the open project Open Whisper Systems. The project released Signal, free encrypted calling for iPhone, on 29 July 2014, and on 2 November 2015 began rolling out Signal for Android, combining its Android apps TextSecure (private messaging) and RedPhone (private calling) in one app.
events.significance: It put strong end-to-end encryption, with keys held on the user's own phone, into a free consumer app designed to be as easy as ordinary texting.

sources.title: Moxie Marlinspike, 'Just Signal'
sources.quote: This is the culmination of our effort to combine TextSecure and RedPhone into one app, which we began on iPhone and are now bringing to completion on Android.
sources.note: The post opens: 'Today we’ve started rolling out Signal for Android, which unites simple private messaging and simple private calling into a single app on Android.' (the page's link markup inserts a space before the comma, so --check was run on the second sentence).

sources.title: Moxie Marlinspike, 'A New Home'
sources.quote: Whisper Systems was a company focused on the development of mobile security software, which was acquired by Twitter in late 2011. Twitter very generously made some of the Whisper Systems software available under an Open Source license (GPLv3), which has since been under open development by the community.
sources.note: Signal for iPhone: 'Free, Worldwide, Encrypted Phone Calls for iPhone', moxie0 on 29 Jul 2014, https://signal.org/blog/signal/ ('today we're releasing Signal – free, worldwide, encrypted voice calls for iPhone, and fully compatible with RedPhone for Android.' — --check FOUND).

events.locationNote: Online-only project. Coordinates: Mountain View, California, the city under which the IRS lists the Signal Technology Foundation (https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/824506840); the foundation was created in 2018, so this is the organisation's later seat, not a verified 2015 office.

events.title: WhatsApp turns on end-to-end encryption for all users
events.place: WhatsApp Inc. (now at Meta Platforms, Menlo Park, California)
events.summary: On 5 April 2016 WhatsApp's founders announced that every call, message, photo, video, file and voice message sent between users of the latest app version, including group chats, was now end-to-end encrypted by default. Open Whisper Systems said the same day that its Signal Protocol integration, begun under a partnership announced in November 2014, was complete across all WhatsApp clients, and that over a billion monthly active users were now using the protocol.
events.significance: Encryption the provider itself cannot read became the default for more than a billion people, shifting the privacy of messages from company policy to keys on users' devices.

sources.title: end-to-end encryption (signed 'Jan and Brian')
sources.quote: From now on when you and your contacts use the latest version of the app, every call you make, and every message, photo, video, file, and voice message you send, is end-to-end encrypted by default, including group chats.
sources.note: The repo helper received HTTP 400 from this site; the page was fetched with curl (HTTP 200) and the helper's --check was run on that copy. Also: 'No one can see inside that message. Not cybercriminals. Not hackers. Not oppressive regimes. Not even us.'

sources.title: Moxie Marlinspike, 'WhatsApp's Signal Protocol integration is now complete'
sources.quote: Over a billion monthly active users across the world are now using the Signal Protocol for end-to-end encryption.
sources.note: Partnership announced 18 Nov 2014: https://signal.org/blog/whatsapp/.

events.locationNote: Online roll-out. Coordinates: Menlo Park, California, where WhatsApp's parent now receives legal notices (WhatsApp terms: '1 Meta Way, Menlo Park, CA 94025'); in April 2016 WhatsApp's own office is reported to have been in nearby Mountain View (not verified).

events.title: A US court orders Apple to help unlock an iPhone; Apple refuses publicly
events.place: U.S. District Court for the Central District of California, Eastern Division, Riverside
events.summary: On 16 February 2016, in case ED No. CM 16-10 (SP), the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California granted the government an order compelling Apple to assist the FBI in searching an iPhone used by San Bernardino shooter Syed Farook, which would have required Apple to write software disabling the phone's auto-erase and passcode delays. The same day Apple's chief executive, Tim Cook, published a letter calling the demand a 'backdoor' and an unprecedented use of the All Writs Act of 1789. On 28 March 2016 the government reported that it had accessed the data without Apple and asked that the order be vacated, leaving the legal question undecided.
events.significance: It tested whether a state can compel a company to break the security of a device whose keys it had deliberately put 'out of our own reach'.

sources.institution: U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of California (filing copy hosted by Prof. Clark D. Cunningham, Georgia State University College of Law)
sources.title: Government's Status Report, In the Matter of the Search of an Apple iPhone…, ED No. CM 16-10 (SP), Document 209
sources.quote: The government has now successfully accessed the data stored on Farook's iPhone and therefore no longer requires the assistance from Apple Inc. mandated by Court's Order Compelling Apple Inc. to Assist Agents in Search dated February 16, 2016.
sources.note: The official justice.gov copy (https://www.justice.gov/usao-cdca/file/836311/download) returned HTTP 401 to scripts. The copy of the 16 February order on the same site is a scanned image without a text layer.

sources.title: Tim Cook, 'A Message to Our Customers'
sources.quote: But now the U.S. government has asked us for something we simply do not have, and something we consider too dangerous to create. They have asked us to build a backdoor to the iPhone.
sources.note: Also: 'Rather than asking for legislative action through Congress, the FBI is proposing an unprecedented use of the All Writs Act of 1789 to justify an expansion of its authority.' and 'We have even put that data out of our own reach, because we believe the contents of your iPhone are none of our business.'

sources.institution: Georgia State University College of Law — FBI v Apple research resource (Prof. Clark D. Cunningham)
sources.title: Cases — In the Matter of the Search of an Apple iPhone (C.D. Cal. No. CM-16-10): iPhone Used by San Bernardino Shooter
sources.quote: A week later, on March 28, the FBI announced that it had been able to access Farook's iPhone and the order against Apple was vacated at the government's request.
sources.note: The page also describes the order as requiring Apple to create 'signed iPhone software' that would disable the auto-erase and time-delay features.

events.locationNote: Coordinates: the federal courthouse in Riverside, seat of the Central District of California's Eastern Division ('ED' in the case number; the case number 5:16-cm-00010 also denotes that division). The U.S. Attorney's filing lists its office in Los Angeles.

events.title: Let's Encrypt leaves beta, making HTTPS certificates free and automatic
events.summary: Let's Encrypt, a free, automated certificate authority run by the nonprofit Internet Security Research Group — founded in May 2013 with Mozilla, the Electronic Frontier Foundation, the University of Michigan, Cisco and Akamai as founding sponsors and partners — was announced on 18 November 2014 and opened a beta in September 2015. On 12 April 2016 it left beta, reporting more than 1.7 million certificates issued for more than 3.8 million websites and stating its aim to 'encrypt 100% of the Web'.
events.significance: Removing the cost and hassle of certificates made encrypted browsing the default, shrinking what networks in the middle can read about ordinary web use.

myths.correction: The name came from 'the onion routing' — the Naval Research Laboratory's original programme. Roger Dingledine used it to distinguish NRL's work from other onion-routing systems; co-designer Paul Syverson says the 2004 paper title 'Tor: The Second-Generation Onion Router' gave an 'implicit impression' of the expansion that is 'simply incorrect'. According to Syverson it was also Dingledine's decision that the name be written 'Tor', not 'TOR'.

sources.institution: U.S. Naval Research Laboratory / ACSAC 2011 (keynote paper, public domain)
sources.title: Paul Syverson, 'A Peel of Onion'
sources.quote: we gave an at least implicit impression that 'Tor' stood for 'the onion router'. This further exacerbated the confusion about the paper's scope and focus, but it is also simply incorrect.
sources.note: Same paper: 'He would respond that it was the onion routing, the original program of projects from NRL. It was Rachel Greenstadt who noted to him that this was a nice acronym and gave Tor its name.'

sources.title: History
sources.quote: To distinguish this original work at NRL from other onion routing efforts that were starting to pop up elsewhere, Roger called the project Tor, which stood for The Onion Routing.

myths.claim: Tor was built by the NSA (or 'the US military') as a surveillance tool.
myths.correction: Onion routing was invented in 1995–96 by David Goldschlag, Michael Reed and Paul Syverson at the U.S. Naval Research Laboratory — not the NSA — to 'separate identification from routing'. Tor itself was designed in the early 2000s by Roger Dingledine and Nick Mathewson of the Free Haven Project with Syverson; its code was released under a free-software licence when the network launched in 2002, the Electronic Frontier Foundation funded the work from 2004, and an independent nonprofit, the Tor Project, took it over in 2006. Navy origins are real; the NSA attribution and the 'spy tool' purpose are not supported by the record.

sources.title: History
sources.quote: That's why in October 2002 when the Tor network was initially deployed, its code was released under a free and open software license.
sources.note: Same page: 'in 1995, David Goldschlag, Michael G. Reed, and Paul Syverson at the U.S. Naval Research Lab (NRL) asked themselves if there was a way to create internet connections that don't reveal who is talking to whom' and 'the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) began funding Roger's and Nick's work on Tor in 2004. In 2006, the Tor Project, Inc., a 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization, was founded'.

sources.institution: USENIX Association, Proceedings of the 13th USENIX Security Symposium
sources.title: R. Dingledine, N. Mathewson and P. Syverson, 'Tor: The Second-Generation Onion Router'
sources.quote: We present Tor, a circuit-based low-latency anonymous communication service.
sources.note: Author affiliations on the paper: Dingledine and Mathewson, 'The Free Haven Project'; Syverson, 'Naval Research Lab'.

sources.institution: U.S. Naval Research Laboratory / ACSAC 2011 (keynote paper, public domain)
sources.title: Paul Syverson, 'A Peel of Onion'
sources.quote: Applications can (and usually should) identify themselves to each other. But, the use of a public network should not automatically reveal the identities of communicating parties. The goal here is anonymous routing, not anonymity.

myths.claim: The Clipper chip was a mandatory government backdoor installed in every American phone.
myths.correction: The White House announced Clipper on 16 April 1993 as a 'voluntary program': a government-designed chip for add-on telephone encryption devices, each with keys deposited in two escrow databases set up by the Attorney General and released for lawful wiretaps. The government bought devices to seed a market and AT&T built one product around it, but industry and the public largely rejected it; critics' fear was that other encryption would eventually be outlawed. The scheme never became mandatory, and by the end of the decade the government had abandoned key escrow.

sources.institution: The White House, Office of the Press Secretary (Clinton White House archive, National Archives)
sources.title: Statement by the Press Secretary (Clipper Chip encryption initiative)
sources.quote: The President today announced a new initiative that will bring the Federal Government together with industry in a voluntary program to improve the security and privacy of telephone communications while meeting the legitimate needs of law enforcement.
sources.note: Also: 'To demonstrate the effectiveness of this new technology, the Attorney General will soon purchase several thousand of the new devices.'

sources.title: Why I Wrote PGP
sources.quote: The government initially claimed that using Clipper would be voluntary, that no one would be forced to use it instead of other types of cryptography.
sources.note: A critic's account; the same essay says 'AT&T put Clipper into its secure voice products' and 'to make Clipper completely effective, the next logical step would be to outlaw other forms of cryptography.'

sources.institution: Matt Blaze (mattblaze.org), author copy of ACSAC 2011 paper
sources.title: Key Escrow from a Safe Distance: Looking Back at the Clipper Chip
sources.quote: By the end of the decade, however, the government gave up.
sources.note: Blaze also records that AT&T was '(and ultimately the only) company to produce a full product based on the ill-fated escrow system', and that 'When the US government learned of AT&T's plans to market the TSD, it worried that criminals might use the devices to thwart wiretaps.'

myths.claim: Matt Blaze's 1994 discovery of the LEAF flaw killed the Clipper chip.
myths.correction: Blaze did show that Clipper's escrow could be bypassed with a 16-bit brute-force search, and the finding made the front page of The New York Times. But Blaze himself argues that his paper at most accelerated Clipper's demise: key escrow faced deeper problems — the risk of a growing database of escrowed keys and the cost of requiring special hardware when encryption was becoming cheap software.

sources.institution: Matt Blaze (mattblaze.org), author copy of ACSAC 2011 paper
sources.title: Key Escrow from a Safe Distance: Looking Back at the Clipper Chip
sources.quote: While my paper may have helped accelerate its demise, key escrow would not have been likely to succeed even if the Clipper escrow mechanism had been more robust than it was.
sources.note: The same section lists 'the problem of securing a growing database of end-user keys' and 'the economic problem' of mandating hardware cryptography.

myths.claim: Bitcoin payments are anonymous and untraceable.
myths.correction: Bitcoin is pseudonymous, not anonymous. Its own white paper says every transaction is announced publicly and privacy depends on keeping public keys unlinked to identities — while conceding that 'some linking is still unavoidable'. A 2013 measurement study clustered addresses and concluded that an agency with subpoena power 'would be well placed to identify who is paying money to whom'.

sources.title: Satoshi Nakamoto, 'Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System', section 10 'Privacy'
sources.quote: As an additional firewall, a new key pair should be used for each transaction to keep them from being linked to a common owner. Some linking is still unavoidable with multi-input transactions, which necessarily reveal that their inputs were owned by the same owner.

sources.institution: ACM Internet Measurement Conference (IMC '13, Barcelona); author copy, UC San Diego
sources.title: S. Meiklejohn et al., 'A Fistful of Bitcoins: Characterizing Payments Among Men with No Names'
sources.quote: Using the dissolution of a large Silk Road wallet and notable Bitcoin thefts as case studies, we demonstrate that an agency with subpoena power would be well placed to identify who is paying money to whom.

myths.claim: Satoshi Nakamoto announced Bitcoin on the cypherpunks mailing list.
myths.correction: The white paper was announced on 31 October 2008 on the Cryptography mailing list (cryptography@metzdowd.com), run on a machine of moderator Perry Metzger's company since 2003 — a separate list from the cypherpunks list that began in 1992, though it drew on the same community.

sources.title: Satoshi Nakamoto, 'Bitcoin P2P e-cash paper'
sources.quote: I've been working on a new electronic cash system that's fully peer-to-peer, with no trusted third party.
sources.note: Archive header: 'Fri Oct 31 14:10:00 EDT 2008'; the page footer reads 'More information about the cryptography mailing list'.

sources.title: Perry E. Metzger, 'ADMIN: The list has moved.'
sources.quote: For the second time in its history, the mailing list has moved -- this time from Wasabi Systems to a machine run by my new company, Metzger, Dowdeswell & Co. LLC

myths.claim: Satoshi Nakamoto has been unmasked as the Australian computer scientist Craig Wright.
myths.correction: In a case brought by the Crypto Open Patent Alliance, England's High Court (Mellor J) declared at the end of the trial in March 2024 — with the written judgment handed down on 20 May 2024 — that Craig Wright is not the author of the Bitcoin white paper and is not Satoshi Nakamoto. The real identity of the pseudonymous author remains unknown.

sources.institution: High Court of Justice of England and Wales, Chancery Division (Mellor J)
sources.title: Crypto Open Patent Alliance v Wright, consequentials judgment [2024] EWHC 1809 (Ch)
sources.quote: First, that I have declared that Dr Wright is not the author of the Bitcoin White Paper nor the owner of copyright in it, is not Satoshi Nakamoto and is not the person who created Bitcoin and not the author of the initial versions of the Bitcoin Source Code.
sources.note: Also: 'On 20 May 2024 (the day the Court handed down its judgment and two months after the Court's declarations)'.

myths.claim: Phil Zimmermann was prosecuted (or indicted) for exporting PGP as a munition.
myths.correction: Zimmermann was the target of a three-year US criminal investigation into the June 1991 Usenet posting of PGP, but he was never charged: on 11 January 1996 the U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of California declined prosecution and closed the case. Zimmermann maintained he did not upload PGP to the Internet himself; he gave it to friends who posted it.

sources.institution: Philip Zimmermann (philzimmermann.com), reproducing the signed news release of defence counsel Philip L. Dubois
sources.title: Significant Moments in PGP's History: Zimmermann Case Dropped
sources.quote: The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of California has decided that your client, Philip Zimmermann, will not be prosecuted in connection with the posting to USENET in June 1991 of the encryption program Pretty Good Privacy. The investigation is closed.

sources.institution: IEEE Computer Society Technical Committee on Security and Privacy, Cipher newsletter
sources.title: Case Closed on Zimmermann PGP Investigation
sources.quote: Zimmermann maintained thoughout the investigation that he did not put the software on the Internet.

sources.title: PGP Marks 10th Anniversary
sources.quote: It was on this day in 1991 that I sent the first release of PGP to a couple of my friends for uploading to the Internet.

myths.claim: Diffie and Hellman were the first people to discover public-key cryptography.
myths.correction: Diffie and Hellman were the first to publish it openly, in 1976. At Britain's GCHQ, James Ellis had proposed 'non-secret encryption', and Clifford Cocks and Malcolm Williamson devised equivalents of RSA and of Diffie–Hellman key exchange in the early 1970s; the work stayed classified until GCHQ announced it in December 1997. GCHQ itself says the academics found key exchange independently 'at almost the same time', and it was the open publication that shaped the public privacy debate.

sources.title: Malcolm Williamson — one of the originators of Public Key Cryptography at GCHQ in the 1970s
sources.quote: This is now known as the Diffie-Hellmann key exchange after the academic researchers who independently found it at almost the same time.
sources.note: Same page: 'Clifford Cocks devised the public-key encryption system now known as RSA, and shortly afterwards Malcolm Williamson devised a method of public key exchange, which allows two parties to obtain a common secret key while communicating only in public.' Undated page; accessed 2026-09-23.

sources.title: James Ellis
sources.quote: The discovery in 1973 remained classified for a long time and was, at first, only made available for official governmental communications.
sources.note: Same page: 'Ellis died on the 25th November 1997 aged 73, ironically just a month before the public announcement of the GCHQ achievement was made.'

myths.claim: Adam Back invented proof-of-work with Hashcash, the idea behind Bitcoin mining.
myths.correction: Back proposed Hashcash in May 1997 to throttle spam and abuse of anonymous remailers, and Bitcoin's white paper cites it. But Cynthia Dwork and Moni Naor had proposed a CPU 'pricing function' against junk mail in 1992 — prior work Back acknowledges he had not known about when he published.

sources.title: Adam Back, 'Hashcash – A Denial of Service Counter-Measure'
sources.quote: At the time of publication of [1] the author was not aware of the prior work by Dwork and Naor in [2] who proposed a CPU pricing function for the application of combatting junk email.
sources.note: Reference [2]: Cynthia Dwork and Moni Naor, 'Pricing via processing or combatting junk mail', Proceedings of Crypto, 1992.

sources.institution: Harvard John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences
sources.title: Pioneer of modern data privacy Cynthia Dwork wins National Medal of Science
sources.quote: Her research has fought email spam and formed the basis of cryptocurrencies.

myths.claim: WhatsApp's end-to-end encryption contains a 'backdoor' that lets Facebook or governments read messages (The Guardian, January 2017).
myths.correction: The Guardian's 13 January 2017 story described a design choice — WhatsApp by default re-encrypts and resends undelivered messages when a contact's key changes, without first asking the sender to verify. Signal's Moxie Marlinspike called the 'backdoor' label false, and after a review by its readers' editor the Guardian extensively amended the article, which now describes 'a design feature' and says systematic surveillance is unlikely.

sources.title: WhatsApp design feature means some encrypted messages could be read by third party (amended article, originally published 13 January 2017)
sources.quote: This article was originally published on 13 January 2017. It has been extensively amended (see endnotes) following a review by the Guardian's readers' editor.
sources.note: Current standfirst: 'Trade-off between security and usability unlikely to permit systematic surveillance, experts say'. The URL slug preserves the original 'backdoor' headline. The date of the amendment was not shown in the fetched text.

sources.title: Moxie Marlinspike, 'There is no WhatsApp "backdoor"'
sources.quote: Today, The Guardian published a story falsely claiming that WhatsApp's end-to-end encryption contains a "backdoor."

myths.claim: 87% of Americans can be uniquely identified by ZIP code, gender and date of birth.
myths.correction: The 87% figure is Latanya Sweeney's estimate from 1990 census data — people who 'likely' had a unique combination. Re-running the analysis on 2000 census data, Philippe Golle (2006) broadly agreed with the finding but put the share at about 63%. The underlying point — that a few 'anonymous' attributes can single out most people — stands; the exact percentage depends on the census year and method.

sources.institution: Carnegie Mellon University, Data Privacy Working Paper 3 (author copy, Data Privacy Lab)
sources.title: Latanya Sweeney, 'Simple Demographics Often Identify People Uniquely'
sources.quote: It was found that 87% (216 million of 248 million) of the population in the United States had reported characteristics that likely made them unique based only on {5-digit ZIP, gender, date of birth}.

sources.institution: ACM Workshop on Privacy in the Electronic Society (WPES '06, Alexandria, Virginia, 30 October 2006); author copy, Stanford
sources.title: Philippe Golle, 'Revisiting the Uniqueness of Simple Demographics in the US Population'
sources.quote: (63% of the US population) than reported in [10].
sources.note: Full sentence (ligatures in the PDF text layer defeat --check on the whole): 'Our results generally agree with the findings of [10], although we find that disclosing one's gender, ZIP code and full date of birth allows for unique identification of fewer individuals (63% of the US population) than reported in [10].' Reference [10] is Sweeney's study; the abstract opens 'According to a famous study [10] of the 1990 census data, 87% of the US population can be uniquely' (--check FOUND).

myths.claim: In Bernstein v. United States the courts settled, as binding appellate precedent, that software source code is speech protected by the First Amendment.
myths.correction: The district court held the export rules unconstitutional (1996, 1997), and a Ninth Circuit panel agreed on 6 May 1999 that they were a prior restraint on scientific expression. But on 30 September 1999 the Ninth Circuit withdrew that panel opinion for rehearing en banc; before the rehearing, the government loosened the regulations in January 2000, and in 2002 the district court dismissed the remaining case on ripeness grounds. The 1999 panel opinion is widely cited, but it was withdrawn and does not stand as binding precedent.

sources.institution: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit (via Public.Resource.Org)
sources.title: Bernstein v. U.S. Department of Justice, 192 F.3d 1308 (9th Cir. 1999) (order granting rehearing en banc)
sources.quote: The three-judge panel opinion, Bernstein v. U.S. Dept. of Justice, 176 F.3d 1132 (9th Cir. 1999), is withdrawn.

sources.title: Bernstein v. United States — Summary of the case status
sources.quote: Before en-banc review could happen, the government added a big exception to the regulations, and the case was sent back to the District Court.
sources.note: Same page: 'At oral argument on 18 October 2002, the government backed away from its regulations. The District Court subsequently dismissed the case on ripeness grounds.'

sources.title: Bernstein v. US Department of Justice (case page)
sources.quote: After four years and one regulatory change, the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that software source code was speech protected by the First Amendment and that the government's regulations preventing its publication were unconstitutional.
sources.note: Cited as an example of the popular version: the summary is accurate about the May 1999 panel ruling but omits its withdrawal.
